analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal agencies from considering climate effects in environmental reviews.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The National Environmental Policy Act requires federal agencies to study the environmental effects of major projects they approve, such as highways, pipelines, and energy facilities, and share that information with the public. This bill would have written climate change out of that process: agencies could no longer tally a project's greenhouse gas emissions or weigh the climate effects of approving it. The bill's own findings argue that project-by-project climate analysis delays construction and jobs and is scientifically imprecise. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies seeking federal approvals for energy, transportation, and construction projects would benefit, because environmental reviews would no longer document or consider their projects' greenhouse gas emissions, reducing a source of analysis, delay, and litigation risk.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would amend compliance with NEPA to exclude consideration of a project's greenhouse gas emissions, the climate effects of those emissions, and mitigation and adaptation measures [S3].

Its findings state that using NEPA as a climate mitigation tool would be costly, cause delays in energy, transportation, and other construction projects, and result in fewer jobs and slower economic growth [S3].

It quotes a February 2010 Council on Environmental Quality statement that linking specific climatological changes to a particular project is difficult to isolate and that agencies should recognize scientific limits in predicting climate effects [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear unaccounted climate costs: federal decisions on major projects would proceed without the agency documenting, predicting, or mitigating the projects' greenhouse gas emissions, and citizens would lose the NEPA information and analysis on those climate impacts.

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently blind the environmental review process to climate effects, so agencies could approve large-emitting projects without ever tallying their greenhouse gas emissions or considering mitigation [S3].

Its savings clause is narrow: it preserves climate consideration only in laws or rules that specifically address greenhouse gases, not in ordinary project reviews, so the routine pathway for climate analysis would be closed off [S3].

Supporters acknowledge in their own findings that the measure is justified partly on scientific-uncertainty grounds, meaning a real, documented effect (cumulative emissions) would go unmeasured in federal decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, narrow benefits to project sponsors—shorter reviews and less litigation exposure—and it cites genuine scientific limits on attributing specific climate outcomes to single projects. But the cost falls broadly: the public would lose the only process that documents the climate effects of federal project decisions, and because the effects are cumulative across many projects, exempting each one individually means the total impact is never assessed. On balance the bill trades public environmental information for industry convenience.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Inhofe introduced the bill on April 20, 2010, with six Republican cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
It never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or House counterpart action, and died at the end of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public: federal environmental reviews retained the requirement to document and consider the climate effects of major projects, since the exemption was never enacted. Energy and construction developers remain subject to that analysis.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept climate analysis in reviews

for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar climate consideration from NEPA reviews

for.name: 6 of 40 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Barrasso, Vitter, Enzi, Risch, Bennett, Roberts)

against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat joined, and the Democratic-majority committee declined to act on it.

industries.note: The bill would have removed greenhouse gas analysis from the federal reviews their projects need, cutting delay and litigation risk. The public would lose the documented climate accounting of federally approved projects.

The bill's findings cite delays in transportation and construction projects from climate-based NEPA review as the burden being removed. Faster approvals would come at the cost of unexamined climate effects.
